While T1189 (Drive-by Compromise) and T1204 (User Execution) are loosely applicable to XSS attacks, they are not ideally matched—T1189 typically involves compromised websites distributing malware, and T1204 refers to social engineering. The more directly relevant techniques would be T1598 (Phishing) for initial reconnaissance or T1598.003 (Spearphishing Link) if applicable, plus T1059.007 (JavaScript) is correctly cited. The investigation also lacks depth in analyzing the Tor exit node indicator—while mentioned as evidence of adversary anonymization, there's no discussion of whether this IP should be correlated against threat intelligence databases or whether Tor usage necessarily indicates higher risk in this context. Consider revising the ATT&CK mappings to more precisely reflect XSS attack tactics and adding threat intelligence correlation analysis to strengthen the citation quality."}

Severity reasoning is well-grounded—appropriately downgrading from critical to medium given successful perimeter blocking. However, citation quality needs improvement: T1189 (Drive-by Compromise) is questionable here since there's no evidence the XSS was delivered to a user's browser or that it compromised anything; T1059.007 (JavaScript) is tangentially relevant but not directly cited in the findings; T1204 (User Execution) is appropriately ruled out in the analysis but then included in ATT&CK mapping anyway, creating inconsistency. Consider aligning technique citations strictly with what was actually observed—perhaps focusing on T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application) which better fits an XSS attack on a web parameter, and removing techniques that the analysis itself suggests did not occur."}
